The measurement uses a **last-6-hour** window rather than the whole-period average, and the difference is big: for #176 chapter 3 T100, the whole-period average is 414k/h but the last 6 hours were 919k/h, a full 2.2×, so projecting the end from the overall average badly underestimates. When speed can be measured it's labeled “measured”; otherwise it falls back to “linear”. Also fixed a timing issue: the shared snapshot needs live data to know the event number, but that often hadn't arrived on page switch, so the load gave up and never retried — people who opened the ranking page directly never saw the shared snapshot.

This version infers it from shop data: the game has sold paid crystal packs containing “only one kind of item”, and that price is its value for the item; new tiers are picked up automatically. Four are currently detected (Virtual Coin 0.267, Wish Fragment 4, LIVE BONUS drink small 8 / large 75 crystals). A unit price only counts if it comes from a tier with “quantity ≥ 10” — practice scores only come in 2-packs, and taking that at face value would make the 100 scores in the “Lv60 free bundle” worth 17,500 crystals (about NT$4,500), which is clearly absurd, so such small packs are never converted and the page says so. The value ranking gains an expandable note listing each unit price and its source item; item cards also show “items worth N crystals”, so you won't wonder why an item's value beats crystals. Also, the smart recommendation's target field now calculates only after you stop typing, so typing a number in budget mode no longer runs the knapsack algorithm five times.

For each event, only earlier events are used to estimate the delay (each of the four candidate rules is scored by its recent hit rate, and the best one is picked); that event is then predicted and compared with what actually happened. The +366-day stretches in the delay history are exactly the years that cross a 2/29 — “same date + 1 year” absorbs that difference naturally. 前一版的「最近 8 期同型態中位數」有系統性低估的問題: The previous “median of the last 8 same-type events” systematically underestimated
前一版的「最近 8 期同型態中位數」有系統性低估的問題。回測 #150～#176: The previous “median of the last 8 same-type events” systematically underestimated. Backtesting #150–#176 one by one showed the median throws away recent high values entirely — for #176 (WL, 12 days) T100, the sample had #170 at 111.32M and #163 at 104.40M, yet the median came out at 65.41M, as if they didn't exist, underestimating overall by 7–23%. After comparing four methods, it now uses a “log-weighted average with a 6-event half-life + same day count only”: all bias falls within 2%, T2000 absolute error drops from 9.8% to 5.7% and T5000 from 12.0% to 4.8%. Weights decay naturally, so there's no longer a cap on the number of events (for #176 the four most recent take 97.8% of the weight). The displayed range still uses the actual spread of the last 8 events, since the range is meant to show dispersion, and numbers that really happened are more meaningful.

Tick your FC/AP charts (702 TW charts, MASTER+APPEND) to compute your Best 30 effective value using the unofficial difficulty table constants (pentatonic V31, AP-based): AP = constant, FC = constant − 1. The layout faithfully recreates Unibot's (MIT) B30 card: three columns by ten rows of cells, difficulty color circle + constant pill + effective value, FULL COMBO/ALL PERFECT badges and a pastel triangle background, drawn on a 2192×3600 high-res canvas and downloadable as PNG in one tap. Enter a player ID to bring in the profile (name/Rank/leader avatar) and cross-check AP/FC totals per difficulty; the TW public API has no per-song results, so results are ticked manually (saved in the browser). The constants table syncs with the spreadsheet daily. Song titles show community Chinese translations (TW doesn't translate titles officially; you can switch back to the original Japanese, and search works in both). The “+/++” constant marks support two modes: symbols (34.9+, 34.9++) or numeric (+ = +0.05; ++ ≈ +0.1, displayed rounded up to the next band but sorted after the real next band); in numeric mode B30 shows three decimals.

原本的控分只是「輸入分數看活動P」的查詢,方向反了: Score control used to be just a lookup — “enter a score, see the event points” — which is backwards
原本的控分只是「輸入分數看活動P」的查詢,方向反了。改成真正的控分:輸入目前活動: Score control used to be just a lookup — “enter a score, see the event points” — which is backwards. It's now real score control: enter your current and target event points and it works out every way to “land exactly” on the difference. **Splitting is allowed** — mixing different live bonus multipliers often hits an exact number more easily than one setup (e.g. a difference of 1,234 has no single-setup solution but 13 solutions in two parts). Each plan lists, per part, whether to use live bonus, how many games, points per game, the song score range and total energy, sorted by least energy. Scores are given as ranges rather than single numbers because event points are rounded down, so anything within the same 20k band gives the same value. If your current bonus can't hit the exact number (event points are integers and may not divide evenly after the live bonus multiplier), it lists the “nearest bonus that can hit exactly”, so you can fine-tune by swapping cards. The difference is capped at 10,000 — beyond that just play normally; score control is for the precise finish. Plans with impossible scores are excluded (solo lives top out around 2.6M).

對快照做「分數只能遞增」的稽核,發現 World Link 活動期間 API 會: Auditing the snapshots for “scores can only increase” revealed that during World Link events the API mixes up main ranking and chapter ranking values: #176's main ranking had 71 score drops, WL chapter 1 had 25 and chapter 3 had 58 (T1000 worst, dropping 40%)

Auditing the snapshots for “scores can only increase” revealed that during World Link events the API mixes up main ranking and chapter ranking values: #176's main ranking had 71 score drops, WL chapter 1 had 25 and chapter 3 had 58 (T1000 worst, dropping 40%). The decisive evidence is that chapter 1's anomalies match the main ranking digit for digit — T2000 at 08-09 19:27 went 1,275,330 → 1,067,467 on both; chapter 3 even showed T3000 higher than T1000, an impossible order. Non-WL #175 and the clean chapter 2 had zero drops, so the contamination follows WL. The fix is a **backward running-min**: scores only go up, so no point should exceed any later value; injected high values get pushed back into a reasonable range, while normal series are completely unaffected (verified on the clean chapter 2: 0.0% changed, latest value untouched). Trend charts, border analysis and measured hourly rates all use the fixed data.

Tap any player on the ranking page to see a new “Game log” under the details: each dot is one game, showing the EP gained, the rank at that moment, and the gap since the previous game (so you can tell back-to-back play from breaks). Step through games with the left/right arrows (it auto-scrolls into place), or filter by time window (24/12/6/3/1 h) or date; each date shows how many games were played that day. Data is sampled every 15 seconds by our own server—the shortest co-op game is about 150 seconds, so every game is caught and no two get merged. Because the game's public data only provides event scores for the top 100, this covers the top 100 (i.e. all public data), counting from when tracking started with no backfill. If the server was ever down, dots in that span may merge several games, and the note will say so.

Pick a song and difficulty and it fetches the official SUS chart file from the asset mirror and draws taps, criticals, flicks (with direction arrows), traces, holds (including ease-in/ease-out curves, visible relay diamonds and attached diamonds) and guide lines, with critical holds and guides in yellow. Each bar line shows the measure number on the left and the cumulative combo up to that point on the right, including the hidden half-beat ticks of holds—calculated per the pjsekai engine's SUS→USC rules and matching the official note counts on five official charts. BPM changes and skill activation points are marked too and can each be hidden. Measures per column are adjustable, oversized images are scaled to fit iOS's canvas area limit, and you can download PNG/JPG or view at full size. You can also upload .sus files exported from Ched/MikuMikuWorld to draw your own charts. Find it in the sidebar's “Mini-games & makers” tabs (next to the stamp maker), the tool cards, and “Chart” in the command palette.

New page “Event data” (Events → Event overview tab): look up any event, switch to current / previous / next in one tap, or search by name or number. It shows the timeline (start, Carnival halftime results, each WL chapter start, close, ranking release, reward distribution, event end, event shop close—see at a glance where things stand), bonus attributes and characters, event cards split into “From gacha” (that gacha's ★4; for WL, each chapter's character card) and “Event shop” (★3/★2 bought with EP), plus the gacha and its rate-up cards, ranking rewards for every tier (titles, crystals, skill practice tickets, materials), WL chapters and Carnival teams. Data is built daily from the TW master by tools/build-event-info.py (ranking rewards require digging through the 26 MB resourceBoxDetails, which a browser can't fetch on its own). The event distribution Gantt chart is rebuilt: a new “Events” mode (each event in a row by unit, plus one row each for mixed and WL), ranges of 12/18/24/36 months or all, fixed-width months that scroll horizontally when too wide, quarter lines and years, this month shaded, today as a dashed line, names written in the bars, colors by gacha type or event type with a legend, hover for details, click a bar to open gacha details or event data, and PNG export. It used dynamic import, which falls under the browser's module rules—any content-type mismatch gets it rejected outright, and browsers differ in strictness. Final border forecasts are no longer just linear extrapolation: they use a “rate profile + progress-based ensemble” model that accounts for growth differences by Taiwan time of day, hours until close and hours since start, then blends 24h/6h measured rates, same-type historical priors and the tier above's trend according to event progress. The site used to run two EP formulas: the classic EP calculator, deck optimizer, ranking studio and song efficiency ranking used “110 + ⌊score/17000⌋ + min(13, ⌊teammates' score/340k⌋),” while the EP calculator and the app used sekai-calculator's scoot method “⌊(score + 0.075 × team power × 5)/17000⌋ + 123.” For the same input the former systematically underestimated by 4–9% (base 193 vs 200 at a score of 1.2M and team power of 300k). The EP calculator is now the reference and all four places use the same function, so the site never shows two different numbers. Inputs changed too: co-op/Carnival used to ask for “teammates' total score” and now ask for “team power”—the new formula counts teammates' contribution in full and derives it from your own team power, so there's no need to guess. The song efficiency ranking also gets a team power field. Six test cases (co-op/Carnival/solo/auto, including survival rate and different energy amounts) were checked one by one against the EP calculator, and the numbers match exactly.

Below the predicted final border there is now an extra “Hist ○○” line: the median final border of the last 8 events of the same type (same event type and length). Hover it to see the full range. **It is not used in the forecast.** Backtested on #175, using the historical median alone as the forecast gave errors of T100 −42%, T1000 −22%, T5000 −13% — far worse than the site’s current extrapolation, so it is shown only for reference. Only the last 8 events are used to avoid inflation (T100 has risen about 2.8× over two years). A median alone can mislead, so the tooltip also shows the range: WL T100 has historically ranged from 36.5M to 111M, a full 3×. The same backtest also measured a systematic underestimate in extrapolation: past 60% of the event, linear extrapolation underestimates T5000 by about 2–6%, T1000 by 10–13% and T100 by 14–22%, and measured-rate extrapolation is slightly worse. This figure is shown on the page as a reminder to treat the forecast as a lower bound, not a guaranteed border.

The Training tab adds a training strategy: pick one or more characters, and the 22 character missions are grouped into eight areas — cards, master rank & skills, leader & lounge, stamps, conversations, plushies & fixtures, costumes & voices, and area items — listing each one’s progress and next threshold, ordering the least-effort next steps and calculating “how many more until you rank up”. Next steps factor in materials (master rank costs from masterLessons, card stories from a fixed table, fixtures from the fixture index, picking the cheapest cards and fixtures); if you have inventory it shows how much is missing, and steps you lack materials for are pushed back. Suggestions include upcoming gachas with new cards of that character, events where that character is a bonus character (with the event deck using them as leader), monthly pass plushie months and Challenge Live score rewards. When Haruki’s public API doesn’t provide mission progress, cards owned, master rank, skills, leader count, area items and fixtures are estimated from raw data (marked “Estimated”), and the rest are marked “Unknown”. The default target is Lv100 (the character rank bonus for BFES card skills caps at Lv100, and the theoretical skill multiplier table also assumes Lv100), and it can be changed. For each character it calculates the least-effort route to the target (which threshold to reach in each mission, total materials, how much is missing); if the target is out of reach, it tells you what level you would reach after doing everything. “Who to train first” ranks characters with BFES cards first, then characters used in theoretical decks, each sorted by EXP left to the target. Gacha pulls are included too: each character lists upcoming gachas with their cards and rate-up cards (BFES gachas marked “Priority”), how much EXP each new card is worth, and how many new cards the missing EXP equals. There is also an “Ask AI for a full strategy” button that hands the computed routes, material inventory, gachas, event bonuses, plushies and Challenge Live to the site assistant (login and an approved account required; uses one quota), which plans pulls and timing together. Priority now follows practical difficulty: leader count → conversations → cards → master rank → skills → other small items (in practice about 1–2 levels combined); materials that are few in number but hard to get (pure wish crystals, miracle gems, gems) push that item later. Wish drops needed to unlock area items Lv10→11 (character items 5, unit/type 15, Virtual Singers 6, Hatsune Miku 1) are included in the route’s materials and shortfall with extra weight, and items needing dream snow globes from Lv16 are pushed further back.
